question: A developer writes `Kettle.java` and later runs the program. Which sequence describes the Java pipeline correctly?
options: `Kettle.java` → JIT compiler (at compile time) → `Kettle.class` → `javac` (at run time) → machine code
`Kettle.java` → `javac` (at run time) → machine code → JVM → `Kettle.class`
`Kettle.java` → `javac` (at compile time) → `Kettle.class` bytecode → JIT compiler inside the JVM (at run time) → machine code
`Kettle.java` → `javac` (at compile time) → machine code stored in `Kettle.class` → the CPU runs the file directly, with no JVM
explanation: Rule: javac runs once at compile time and turns source into bytecode (.class); the JIT lives inside the JVM and turns bytecode into machine code only while the program runs. So javac never produces machine code, and the JIT never runs at compile time.

question: `Ledger.class` already exists. You type `java Ledger`. Which of the following happen DURING this command? (Select all that apply.)
options: The JVM starts and loads the bytecode in `Ledger.class`
`javac` recompiles `Ledger.java` into native machine code
The JIT compiler translates frequently run bytecode into native machine code
`Ledger.class` is rewritten to hold machine code, so the next run skips the JVM
explanation: Rule: `java X` launches the JVM, which loads bytecode, and its JIT compiles hot bytecode into machine code in memory at run time. javac is not involved when you run a program, and the .class file always stays as portable bytecode.

question: A lab PC has ONLY a JRE installed. A student copies `Quiz.java` and a `Quiz.class` that was compiled on another machine. What happens with each command?
options: Both `javac Quiz.java` and `java Quiz` work, because the JRE contains the compiler
Neither works, because a JRE has no JVM
`javac Quiz.java` works, but `java Quiz` fails because the JIT compiler only comes with the JDK
`javac Quiz.java` fails because `javac` comes with the JDK; `java Quiz` works because the JRE contains the JVM
explanation: Rule: JRE = JVM + libraries (enough to RUN bytecode); JDK = JRE + development tools such as javac (needed to COMPILE). The JIT is part of the JVM, so a JRE has it; what a JRE is missing is javac.

question: `Meter.java` has two bugs: (1) a missing semicolon, and (2) a division by zero that only happens when the user enters 0. Who reports each bug, and when?
options: (1) is reported by the JIT compiler at compile time; (2) is reported by `javac`
(1) is reported by `javac` while compiling, and no .class file is produced; (2) is reported at run time by the JVM as an ArithmeticException
Both are reported by `javac`, because javac produces machine code and checks how it will run
(1) is reported by the JVM when it loads `Meter.java`; (2) is reported by `javac`
explanation: Rule: syntax and type errors are compile-time errors found by javac (step .java → .class); errors that depend on input values happen at run time inside the JVM. The JIT only works on bytecode that already compiled, so it never reports syntax errors.

question: Which of these can be thrown with `throw new X();` from a method that has NO try/catch and NO `throws` clause, and still compile? (Select all that apply.)
options: `FileNotFoundException`
`OutOfMemoryError`
`InterruptedException`
`ClassCastException`
explanation: Rule: unchecked = RuntimeException and its subclasses PLUS Error and its subclasses; only these need no catch or throws. OutOfMemoryError is an Error and ClassCastException is a RuntimeException, while FileNotFoundException (an IOException) and InterruptedException are checked.

question: Which of these are CHECKED exceptions, which the compiler forces you to catch or declare? (Select all that apply.)
options: `StackOverflowError`
`Exception` (plain)
`NumberFormatException`
`CloneNotSupportedException`
explanation: Rule: a Throwable is checked unless it is a RuntimeException or an Error (or a subclass of either). StackOverflowError is unchecked because it is an Error, even though it is not a RuntimeException; NumberFormatException extends IllegalArgumentException, which is a RuntimeException. Plain Exception and CloneNotSupportedException are checked.

question: What is the result of compiling this code?
options: Only line R is a compile error: unreported exception Exception; must be caught or declared to be thrown
Lines P and R are compile errors, because neither `open` nor `reset` declares `throws`
No errors: it compiles and prints `bad pin`, because `main` catches Exception
Lines Q and R are compile errors, because `new Exception` cannot be thrown directly
explanation: Rule: a method that throws a checked exception must catch it or declare it itself; a catch in the CALLER does not fix the method that throws. Line Q is fine because `lock()` declares `throws Exception`, and line P is fine because IllegalArgumentException is unchecked.

question: What happens when this code is compiled and run?
options: Compile error: `parsePort` must declare `throws NumberFormatException, IllegalArgumentException`
Compile error: `main` must call `parsePort` inside a try/catch
It compiles, prints `80`, then the program ends with an uncaught NumberFormatException
It compiles and prints `80`, then `done`, because unchecked exceptions are ignored
explanation: Rule: unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException subclasses such as NumberFormatException) need no try/catch and no throws to COMPILE, but they still stop the program at run time if nothing catches them. So it compiles, and `done` is never printed.

question: What is printed?
options: 1 2 4, then the program ends with an uncaught IllegalStateException
explanation: Rule: an exception thrown inside a catch block is NOT handled by the sibling catches of the same try; finally runs, then the exception propagates to the caller. Here `main` catches it (an IllegalStateException is a RuntimeException), so `6 7` is printed, but `3` and `5` are skipped.

question: What is printed?
options: ABDFGH
ABDG, then the program ends with an uncaught UnsupportedOperationException
ABCDGH
ABCDEGH
explanation: Rule: an exception thrown inside a catch block CAN be caught by a try/catch nested inside that same catch block, just not by its sibling catches. The inner catch prints C, the inner finally prints D, the outer catch carries on with E, and then the outer finally (G) and H run normally.

question: What is printed?
options: caught wrapped
caught bad
fallback
Compile error: the throw in the catch block makes the return unreachable
explanation: Rule: finally always runs, and a `return` inside finally replaces whatever was in flight, including an exception that is propagating, so that exception is silently discarded. The RuntimeException from the catch block is thrown away and `fetch()` returns normally with "fallback".

question: What happens when this runs?
options: Prints `N F `, then the program ends with an uncaught ArithmeticException
Prints `N A F End`
Prints `N E F End`
Prints `N R F End`
explanation: Rule: the catch blocks of a try only guard the try block, never each other, so an ArithmeticException thrown inside `catch (NumberFormatException e)` skips the matching-looking `catch (ArithmeticException e)` and even `catch (Exception e)`. finally prints F, then the exception leaves `main` uncaught and `End` never prints.

question: Class `Ticket` shows the attribute lines below (styling described in brackets). Select ALL lines where the Java translation is correct.
options: `# price : double` → `private double price;`
`~ zone : String` → `String zone;` (no access modifier)
`- nextId : int` [underlined] → `private static int nextId;`
`# seat : int` [underlined] → `protected final int seat;`
explanation: Rule: `+` public, `-` private, `#` protected, `~` package (no modifier in Java); underlined = static; italic = abstract. `#` is protected, not private, and underline means static, not final.

question: Class `Hotel` declares `protected static int maxGuests;`. Which UML attribute line shows it correctly?
options: `~ maxGuests : int`, drawn underlined
`# maxGuests : int`, drawn underlined
`# maxGuests : int`, drawn in italics
`+ maxGuests : int`, drawn underlined
explanation: Rule: protected → `#`, and static → underlined (italics means abstract). `~` is package visibility (no modifier), which is a different access level from protected even though both allow access within the same package.

question: In class `Cart`, the operation `+getTotal() : double` is drawn UNDERLINED (Mermaid shows this with `$`). Which Java matches it?
options: `public double getTotal() { ... }`, an ordinary instance method; the underline only marks a query method
`public abstract double getTotal();`
`public static double getTotal() { ... }`, called as `Cart.getTotal()` without needing an object
`public final double getTotal() { ... }`
explanation: Rule: underlining an attribute OR an operation means static (class scope); italics would mean abstract. Underline never means final, so this is a public static method that belongs to the class, not to each Cart object.

question: Which UML class box matches this Java code?
options: Class name `Shipment` plain; `+ ref : String`; `+ cost() : double` underlined
Class name `Shipment` plain; `- ref : String`; `~ cost() : double` underlined
Class name `Shipment` in italics; `# ref : String`; `# cost() : double` in italics
Class name `Shipment` in italics; `~ ref : String`; `~ cost() : double` in italics
explanation: Rule: italic = abstract (for the class name and for abstract operations), and no Java modifier means package visibility, written `~`. Option C is tempting, but `#` means protected, which needs the `protected` keyword in Java.

question: Following the slides' rules, how many DASHED dependency arrows should leave `Barista` (counting Grinder, Order, Receipt and Timer)?
options: 3 (Order, Receipt, Timer)
4 (all of them)
1 (Timer only)
2 (Order and Timer)
explanation: Rule: a class held in a FIELD is an association (solid line); a class used only as a parameter, a return type or a local variable is a dependency (dashed arrow). Grinder is a field, so it is the only solid line. The return type Receipt counts as a dependency, even though it is easy to forget.

question: What is printed?
options: right left down up
left right Zed Zed
left right up down
left right down up
explanation: Rule: Java passes a COPY of each reference; reassigning a parameter (`a = b`, `p = new ...`) never affects the caller, but changing an object THROUGH the reference (`p[0] = ...`) does. So x and y are unchanged, the array's elements really are swapped, and `rename` only repoints its local copy.

question: This whole file is saved as **Garden.java** and you run `javac Garden.java`, then `java Garden`. What happens?
options: It compiles to `Flower.class`, `Garden.class` and `Tree.class`, and `java Garden` prints `ok`
Compile error: a .java file may contain only one class
It compiles, but only `Garden.class` is produced; Flower and Tree are discarded
Compile error: `Flower` and `Tree` must also be declared public
explanation: Rule: a file may hold at most ONE public class, and that class's name must match the file name; non-public classes can sit in the same file under any name. javac writes one .class file per class.

question: How should the two whole-part relationships in this code be drawn?
options: Score-Page: hollow diamond at Score; Orchestra-Musician: filled diamond at Orchestra
Score-Page: filled diamond at Score; Orchestra-Musician: hollow diamond at Orchestra
Score-Page: filled diamond at Page; Orchestra-Musician: hollow diamond at Musician
Both use a filled diamond (at Score and at Orchestra), because both keep their parts in a field
explanation: Rule: parts CREATED inside the whole (lifetime owned by the whole) = composition, a filled diamond; parts PASSED IN from outside = aggregation, a hollow diamond. The diamond always sits at the WHOLE end. Holding the parts in a field only tells you it is more than a dependency.

question: A team tries to reuse its `PaymentGateway` module in a sister project, but cannot, because the module drags along the UI, logging and reporting packages it depends on. Which slide symptom is this, and which design goal has it failed?
options: Rigidity; it fails Extensibility
Fragility; it fails Maintainability
Rigidity; it fails Reusability
Immobility; it fails Reusability
explanation: Rule: the goals are Reusability, Extensibility and Maintainability; the symptoms of rotting design are Rigidity (hard to change, cascading changes), Fragility (breaks in unrelated places) and Immobility (cannot be reused because of too much baggage). Being unable to lift the module into another project is Immobility, the opposite of Reusability.

question: Which statement about these marked lines is correct?
options: L5 is a compile error. If L5 is removed, the program compiles, L4 is fine, and L3 throws ArrayStoreException at run time
L1 and L5 are compile errors, because neither an Apple[] nor a List<Apple> is a kind of Fruit container
L4 and L5 are compile errors; L3 runs fine because a Banana is a Fruit
L3 is a compile error, and L5 compiles because Apple extends Fruit
explanation: Rule: arrays are covariant (an Apple[] IS a Fruit[]), so storing the wrong subtype is only caught at run time with ArrayStoreException; generics are invariant (List<Apple> is NOT a List<Fruit>), so that is caught at compile time. A wildcard `List<? extends Fruit>` is the legal way to view a List<Apple>.

question: Because of type erasure, which marked lines FAIL to compile?
options: L4 and L7 only
L1, L4, L5 and L7
L1, L4 and L7 only
L1, L4, L5, L6 and L7
explanation: Rule: T is erased at run time, so anything that needs the actual type of T at run time is illegal: `new T()`, `new T[...]`, `instanceof List<String>`, and a `static T` field (static members belong to the class, not to any one Registry<T>). Casting to `(T[])` compiles; it only gives an unchecked warning.

question: Which statement best diagnoses this design?
options: It violates LSP because the pre-condition is stronger: `BudgetDispenser` rejects requests above 10
No violation: a subclass may narrow behaviour, as long as the override compiles
It violates LSP because the post-condition is weaker: callers that rely on getting exactly `pills` pills can get fewer
It violates the Interface Segregation Principle, because `Dispenser` has a method that the subclass does not fully support
explanation: Rule (design by contract): an overriding method's pre-conditions must be no stronger (expect no more) and its post-conditions no weaker (provide no less). It still accepts every input, so the pre-condition is unchanged, but it delivers less than the base promises, which is a weaker post-condition. Compiling is not the same as being substitutable.
